identifies_rows: The KEY identifies a row. The id (R1, R2, ...) is assigned by position in this file and means nothing outside it.
instructions: your_value -- the number the source states. If sources disagree, give the range AND the rule you used to reduce it (for example "2.5-2.7, took the midpoint to two significant figures").
source -- the authority you consulted, specific enough to find again.

citation_correct -- about the code's cited source only, carried on each row as "cited". Answer it separately from the value: a right number under a wrong authority is a real finding and one token cannot say it.
notes -- anything a token cannot carry. The checker reads notes as prose for a human, never as a verdict.

One token per verdict field. A field holding a token plus a qualification is reported as unclassified rather than read, because guessing which half you meant is the interpretation this system is built to avoid.
row_hash: sha256 over key, claim and code value, first 8 hex characters. Do not edit those three fields; the checker recomputes this and a row whose hash is missing or wrong is returned rather than read.
selection_why: constants_new.py only -- the pilot slice (L-201). Its branch coverage is a property of the file, not of anyone's judgement about which rows are interesting.

cited: IAU 2012 Resolution B2 -- exact definition
notes: The code value is the exact IAU definition expressed in kilometres.
source: IAU 2012 Resolution B2, recommendation 1 (astronomical unit = 149,597,870,700 m exactly).

cited: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 -- nominal solar radius
notes: This is a nominal conversion constant, exact by definition; it is not a measurement of the instantaneous solar photospheric radius.
source: IAU 2015 Resolution B3, recommendation 3, Table 1 (nominal solar conversion constant R_sun^N = 6.957×10^8 m exactly).

cited: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 -- nominal terrestrial equatorial radius
notes: 6378.137 km is the GRS80 reference-ellipsoid semi-major axis. IAU 2015 Resolution B3 instead defines the nominal terrestrial equatorial radius as 6378.1 km, so the number is standard but the code's cited authority is wrong.
source: Moritz, Geodetic Reference System 1980, Bulletin Géodésique 54 (1980), definition adopted by IUGG Resolution 7 (equatorial radius a = 6,378,137 m).

cited: IERS Conventions (Petit & Luzum 2010); IAU B3 rounds to 6356.8 km
notes: The IERS Table 1.1 parameters give b = 6356.751858 km, which rounds to the code's 6356.752 km. IAU 2015 Resolution B3 separately defines a nominal terrestrial polar radius of 6356.8 km.
source: Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, Table 1.1 (a_E = 6378136.6 m and 1/f = 298.25642; polar radius derived from those defining ellipsoid parameters).

cited: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 -- nominal jovian equatorial radius
notes: This is an exact nominal conversion constant, not a newly measured 1-bar radius.
source: IAU 2015 Resolution B3, recommendation 3, Table 1 (nominal jovian equatorial radius R_eJ^N = 7.1492×10^7 m exactly).

cited: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 -- nominal jovian polar radius
notes: This is an exact nominal conversion constant, not a newly measured 1-bar radius.

cited: NIST/SI exact definition
notes: The value is exact in SI; conversion from m/s to km/s is exact.
source: NIST Special Publication 330 (2019), §2.2 and Table 1, The International System of Units (SI), 9th-edition SI Brochure text (c = 299,792,458 m/s exactly).

cited: Carroll & Ostlie, An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics, Ch. 11 -- chromosphere extends ~2000 km above the photosphere.
notes: The 2000 km figure is a conventional approximate thickness, not a sharply defined physical boundary; NASA's NSSDCA Sun Fact Sheet uses ~2500 km. I could not directly inspect the cited Carroll & Ostlie Ch. 11 passage.
source: Nindos et al., 'The dynamic chromosphere at millimeter wavelengths,' Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences 9 (2022), §1 (chromosphere traditionally defined as a ~2000-km-thick layer); NASA Imagine the Universe, 'The Chromosphere' (extends about 2000 km from the photosphere).

cited: Golub & Pasachoff, "The Solar Corona" (2010)
notes: Coronal-region boundaries are conventional rather than physical constants. The 2023 community consensus places the inner-to-middle-corona boundary at about 1.5 R_sun, not 3 R_sun. I could not directly inspect Golub & Pasachoff (2010) for a 3 R_sun definition.
source: West et al., 'Defining the Middle Corona,' Solar Physics 298:78 (2023), Abstract and §1 (community consensus defines the middle corona as approximately 1.5-6 R_sun from disk center, with the inner corona below that inner boundary).

cited: Golub & Pasachoff (2010); DeForest, Howard & McComas (2014), ApJ 787:124
context_only: See: Eclipse observations; helmet streamers extend 4-6 R_sun
notes: The paper uses 6 R_sun as an observational distance beyond which inbound waves were detected, not as a fixed outer radius of the streamer belt. A streamer belt has no single hard radial boundary.
source: DeForest, Howard & McComas, 'Inbound waves in the solar corona: a direct indicator of Alfvén Surface location,' Astrophysical Journal 787:124 (2014), Abstract (inbound wave motion detected beyond 6 R_sun; lower bound on the Alfvén surface 17 R_sun in the streamer belt).

cited: Murray & Dermott, "Solar System Dynamics" (1999), Sec. 4.6
context_only: Derived: Fluid Roche limit formula: d = 2.44 * R * (rho_sun/rho_comet)^(1/3)
Calculation: 2.44 * 1.0 * (1408/500)^(1/3) = 3.45 R_sun Using rho_sun = 1408 kg/m3, rho_comet ~ 500 kg/m3
notes: The cited section is wrong: §4.6 is the Darwin-Radau relation; the Roche discussion is §4.8. Using 2.46 gives 3.47 R_sun; using the code note's 2.44 gives 3.45 R_sun. The result is model- and assumed-density-dependent.
source: Murray & Dermott, Solar System Dynamics (1999), §4.8 'The Roche Zone' (hydrostatic Roche coefficient 2.46); using rho_sun = 1408 kg/m^3 and rho_comet = 500 kg/m^3 gives 3.47 R_sun.

cited: Kasper et al. (2021), Phys. Rev. Lett. 127:255101
context_only: See: Parker Solar Probe first crossing, April 28, 2021
notes: 18.8 R_sun is the location of the first observed crossing, not a fixed spherical Alfvén-surface radius; the surface is structured and time-variable. The PRL abstract itself gives the location in kilometres rather than stating 18.8 R_sun.
source: NASA Goddard, 'NASA Enters the Solar Atmosphere for the First Time, Bringing New Discoveries' (14 Dec 2021), section 'Closer Than Ever Before' (first crossing reported at 18.8 solar radii); Kasper et al., Physical Review Letters 127:255101 (2021), Abstract (same 28 Apr 2021 crossing, reported as 13 million km above the photosphere).
